Pluck a string and you get a note you could hum. Strike a drum and you get a thud. Both are a stretched piece of material, set shaking. So why do they sound so different?

## The answer in three steps

**1. Everything that vibrates has a set of favorite shapes.** A string can swing as one arc, as two halves moving in opposite directions, as three thirds, and so on. Each of these shapes, called a [mode](glossary.qmd#mode), swings at its own frequency.

```{=html}
<svg class="fig" viewBox="0 0 320 112" role="img" aria-label="The first three modes of a string: one arc, two halves, three thirds, at 1, 2 and 3 times the lowest frequency"><path class="dash" d="M 40 22 L 280 22"/><path class="acc" d="M 40 22 C 126.4 7.7 193.6 7.7 280.0 22"/><path class="acc" opacity="0.35" d="M 40 22 C 126.4 36.3 193.6 36.3 280.0 22"/><circle cx="40" cy="22" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><circle cx="280" cy="22" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><text x="290" y="26">1×</text><path class="dash" d="M 40 56 L 280 56"/><path class="acc" d="M 40 56 C 83.2 41.7 116.8 41.7 160.0 56 C 203.2 70.3 236.8 70.3 280.0 56"/><path class="acc" opacity="0.35" d="M 40 56 C 83.2 70.3 116.8 70.3 160.0 56 C 203.2 41.7 236.8 41.7 280.0 56"/><circle cx="40" cy="56" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><circle cx="280" cy="56" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><text x="290" y="60">2×</text><path class="dash" d="M 40 90 L 280 90"/><path class="acc" d="M 40 90 C 68.8 75.7 91.2 75.7 120.0 90 C 148.8 104.3 171.2 104.3 200.0 90 C 228.8 75.7 251.2 75.7 280.0 90"/><path class="acc" opacity="0.35" d="M 40 90 C 68.8 104.3 91.2 104.3 120.0 90 C 148.8 75.7 171.2 75.7 200.0 90 C 228.8 104.3 251.2 104.3 280.0 90"/><circle cx="40" cy="90" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><circle cx="280" cy="90" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><text x="290" y="94">3×</text></svg>
```

**2. A pluck sets many of them going at once.** What you hear is a chord of the modes' frequencies: the lowest, called the [fundamental](glossary.qmd#fundamental), and the [overtones](glossary.qmd#partial) above it. They are the stems on the ruler above.

**3. Whether that chord sounds like one note depends on how the frequencies line up.** If they sit at, or very near, whole-number multiples of one frequency in the range we hear as pitch, the sound repeats itself many times a second, and the ear hears that repetition rate as the [pitch](glossary.qmd#pitch). A string's modes do exactly that: 1×, 2×, 3×, …. An ideal drumhead's land at 1×, 1.59×, 2.14×, 2.30×, …: a few fall near a line by chance, but no frequency we hear as pitch fits them all. The sound doesn't repeat at any rate we hear as pitch, and it dies fast: a thud.

::: {.northstar}
**The idea behind the whole series.** Newton's law turns each instrument into an [operator], and the operator's [spectrum](glossary.qmd#spectrum) gives its frequencies: how the instrument is built, stretched and held decides them. Put the frequencies you hear on the pitch ruler: **on the lines, a note; off the lines, a clang or a thud.** More exactly, you hear a note when they all sit at, or very near, whole-number multiples of one frequency in the range we hear as pitch. Each instrument page puts its instrument on the ruler to see which.
:::

## The mathematics: one recipe, every instrument

Behind every page is the same recipe, and it is the mathematical heart of the series: Newton's law gives each instrument an operator, and the operator's spectrum gives its frequencies. The page [The spectrum of an operator](spectrum.qmd) lays the idea out in full and runs it on every instrument; here are its two steps.

**1. Derive the instrument's operator from first principles.** Take one small piece of the instrument (a bit of string, a slab of air, a slice of steel, a patch of drumhead) and apply Newton's law: mass times acceleration equals the force on it. The force comes from the material: tension, air pressure, or the stiffness of bent steel. Worked out, the force on the piece turns out to depend only on the shape of the instrument around it, through a fixed rule. Dividing by the mass gives an equation of the same form for every instrument,
$$
u_{tt} = -A\,u ,
$$
where $u$ is the instrument's shape (how far each point is from rest; for a tube, the air pressure), $u_{tt}$ is its [acceleration](glossary.qmd#partial-derivative), and $A$ is the [operator]: the rule that takes a shape and returns minus the restoring force per unit mass. How the instrument is held (ends tied, clamped, open, free) decides which shapes $A$ may act on, and is part of the operator.

**2. Find its spectrum.** A [mode](glossary.qmd#mode) is a shape that the operator only rescales,
$$
A\,X = \lambda\,X ,
$$
for some number $\lambda$, an [eigenvalue](glossary.qmd#eigenvalue). Every operator here has $\lambda \ge 0$ (where $\lambda = 0$ occurs, it is the whole instrument drifting, which makes no sound). For $\lambda > 0$ such a shape swings in place as $X\cos(\sqrt{\lambda}\,t + \phi)$, so it sounds at the frequency
$$
f = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda}}{2\pi} .
$$
The list of all the eigenvalues is the operator's [spectrum](glossary.qmd#spectrum). So the frequencies an instrument rings at on its own, once struck or plucked, are fixed by its operator; how you strike or pluck it only decides how strongly each one sounds. A steady bow or breath can do more: it can lock the sound onto exact whole-number multiples (pages 4, 5 and 6b).

Each instrument page carries out both steps in full, from Newton's law to the frequencies:

| Page | Newton's law on | Operator $A$ | Held | Frequencies |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| [1 · Spring](oscillator.qmd) | one mass | multiply by $k/m$ | — | one: $\sqrt{k/m}/2\pi$ |
| [2 · Beads](ring.qmd) | each bead | a matrix | in a ring | $\propto \sin(\pi k/N)$ |
| [3 · Loop](circle.qmd) | a bit of string | $-c^2\,d^2/d\theta^2$ | in a loop | $\propto n$, exactly |
| [4 · String](violin.qmd) | a bit of string | $-c^2\,d^2/dx^2$ | both ends tied | $\propto n$ |
| [5 · Clarinet](clarinet.qmd) | a slab of air | $-c^2\,d^2/dx^2$, on pressure | one end closed | $\propto 2n-1$ |
| [6 · Kalimba](kalimba.qmd) | a slice of steel | $\kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4$ | clamped, free tip | $1 : 6.27 : 17.55$ |
| [7 · Piano](piano.qmd) | a bit of stiff wire | $-c^2\,d^2/dx^2 + \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4$ | ends pinned | $n\sqrt{1+Bn^2}$, slightly sharp |
| [8 · Drum](drum.qmd) | a patch of drumhead | $-c^2\,\Delta$ | rim fixed | $1 : 1.59 : 2.14 : 2.30$ |

Here $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ counts the modes, $N$ is the number of beads, $\Delta$ is the two-dimensional version of $d^2/dx^2$ (page 8), and $\propto$ means "proportional to". The constants $c$, $\kappa$ and $B$ come from tension, density and stiffness; each page derives them. The [map](map.qmd) has the full comparison.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>What counts as a note <span class="needs">uses no extra mathematics</span></summary>

A clear pitch means the frequencies you hear sit at, or very near, whole-number multiples of one frequency in the pitch range, from a few dozen to a few thousand hertz. That frequency need not be present itself (page 0). Then the sound repeats, or nearly repeats, and the repetition rate is the pitch. What you hear can differ from the spectrum in two ways: some frequencies die almost at once, leaving the rest (the kalimba, page 6), and a steady bow or breath can lock the motion into exact repetition near one of the operator's frequencies, even when the operator's overtones are off the lines (the harmonica, page 6b).

</details>
:::

[operator]: glossary.qmd#operator

The demo sounds in this list are simplified: the piano pair exaggerates the string's stiffness, and the two drums play every mode equally loud.

Short on time? Start with [the spectrum of an operator](spectrum.qmd), the idea in one page. Or read each page's puzzle and the short summary box under its demo: about half an hour for the whole series. Or pages 0, 4 and 8, the note, the string and the drum, carry the main idea, and 4 and 8 derive their operators and spectra in full; page 3 shows the recipe in its simplest form. The [map](map.qmd) has every instrument's sound side by side, reading paths by depth, and the reference tables. Blue words link to the [glossary](glossary.qmd).

```{=html}
<script src="core.js"></script>
<script>
(function () {
  "use strict";
  var C = Core, M = C.models;
  function fadeOut(buf, sec) { var d = buf.getChannelData(0), n = Math.floor(sec * buf.sampleRate); for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) d[d.length - 1 - i] *= i / n; return buf; }
  // ---- the opening pair: a plucked string and a struck drum, on the pitch ruler ----
  var HOOK = {
    string: { parts: function () { return M.violin.partials({ pluck: 0.2 }); }, f: 196, dur: 2.6, svg: "rulerString" },
    drum: { parts: function () { return M.drum.partials({ r: 0.35 }); }, f: 140, dur: 2.4, svg: "rulerDrum" }
  };
  function drawRulers() {
    Object.keys(HOOK).forEach(function (k) {
      C.stems(document.getElementById(HOOK[k].svg), HOOK[k].parts(), { W: 320, H: 96, rmax: 6, fs: 9, sw: 2.5, noOff: true });
    });
  }
  document.querySelectorAll("[data-hook]").forEach(function (b) {
    b.addEventListener("click", function () { var h = HOOK[b.getAttribute("data-hook")]; C.play(C.render(C.toHz(h.parts(), h.f), h.dur), 0.75); });
  });
  // ---- the six puzzles ----
  function harmonics(f, n, odd, skip1) { var out = []; for (var k = 1; k <= n; k++) { if (odd && k % 2 === 0) continue; if (skip1 && k === 1) continue; out.push({ f: f * k, amp: 1 / k, tau: 10 }); } return out; }
  // Octave puzzle: simplified stiff-string notes, only the lowest partials, so the tuner's 2 : 1 beat (C4's 2nd partial against C5) stands out.
  var BS = 0.0024, LOW = 261.63, P2 = Math.sqrt((1 + 4 * BS) / (1 + BS));
  function stiffNote(f1, amps) { return amps.map(function (a, i) { var n = i + 1; return { f: f1 * n * Math.sqrt((1 + BS * n * n) / (1 + BS)), amp: a, tau: 3 }; }); }
  var GWW = [2.53794399980, 3.65550971352, 5.17555935622, 6.53755744376, 7.24807786256, 9.20929499840, 10.5969856913, 11.5413953956, 12.3370055014, 13.0536540557, 14.3138624643, 15.8713026200];
  function gww() { return GWW.map(function (v, k) { return { f: 150 * Math.sqrt(v / GWW[0]), amp: 1, tau: 1.4 / (1 + 0.12 * k) }; }); }
  var G = {
    string: function () { return C.render(C.toHz(M.violin.partials({ pluck: 0.2 }), 196), 2.6); },
    drum: function () { return C.render(C.toHz(M.drum.partials({ r: 0.35 }), 140), 2.4); },
    note: function () { return fadeOut(C.render(harmonics(220, 8), 1.6), 0.3); },
    nofund: function () { return fadeOut(C.render(harmonics(220, 8, false, true), 1.6), 0.3); },
    flute: function () { return fadeOut(C.render(harmonics(343 / 1.2, 8), 1.6), 0.3); },
    clar: function () { return fadeOut(C.render(harmonics(343 / 2.4, 15, true), 1.6), 0.3); },
    kal: function () { return C.render(C.toHz(M.kalimba.partials(), 523.25), 2.4); },
    harm: function () { return fadeOut(C.render(C.toHz(M.harmonica.partials(), 523.25), 1.6), 0.3); },
    oct: function () { return C.render(stiffNote(LOW, [1, 0.7, 0.3]).concat(stiffNote(2 * LOW, [0.7, 0.25])), 4); },
    str: function () { return C.render(stiffNote(LOW, [1, 0.7, 0.3]).concat(stiffNote(2 * LOW * P2, [0.7, 0.25])), 4); },
    gA: function () { return C.render(gww(), 2.4); },
    gB: function () { return C.render(gww(), 2.4); }
  };
  document.querySelectorAll("[data-g]").forEach(function (b) {
    b.addEventListener("click", function () { C.play(G[b.getAttribute("data-g")](), 0.75); });
  });
  C.onTheme(drawRulers);
  drawRulers();
})();
</script>
```
